passages.t: A fountain of tears, and tongues like bows
passages.happening:
“Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears!” (verse 1). The prophet wishes he could weep day and night for the slain of his people. Yet in the next breath he wishes for a traveler's lodge in the wilderness, so he could leave them all behind, for they are faithless (verse 2).

God says they bend their tongues like bows; lies prevail over truth (verse 3). Everyone must guard against his neighbor and trust no brother, for every friend spreads slander (verse 4). ‘They have taught their tongues to lie’ (verse 5). ‘With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him’ (verse 8). So God will refine and test them (verse 7).

The prophet laments for the scorched pastures where no cattle low (verse 10). God will make Jerusalem a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals (verse 11). Who is wise enough to understand why? Because they forsook God's law and followed the stubbornness of their hearts and the Baals (verses 12 to 14). So God will feed them wormwood, scatter them among the nations, and send a sword after them (verses 15 and 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter belongs to the reign of Jehoiakim, from 609 to 598 BC, when Judah was caught between Egypt and Babylon and its leaders were divided over which to trust. In times like that, informers, factions and self-interest can make every relationship dangerous. Jeremiah would soon find his own family and townspeople plotting against him.

The traveler's lodge in the wilderness was a simple shelter for caravans on desert roads, the loneliest place a person could go. Jeremiah would rather be there than among his own people. He weeps for them and wants to escape them, both at once.

Wormwood was a bitter plant, a byword for anything bitter. Poisoned water was the opposite of the living water of chapter 2.
passages.later: The psalms pray against the same sin: ‘who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts’ (Psalm 28:3). Lamentations, after the fall, finds Jerusalem as verse 11 said: ‘Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes’ (Lamentations 5:18).
passages.hard:
Verse 16 says God will send a sword after his people until he has finished them, but elsewhere he says he will not make a full end. Which is it?

Jeremiah contains both kinds of statement. Verse 16 speaks of a sword sent until they are consumed. Yet 4:27 and 5:10, 18 say God will not make a full end, and chapters 29 to 33 promise return and restoration. Many interpreters see a difference between the nation as a political and religious order, which did end in 586 BC, and the people as a whole, a remnant of whom would survive and return. Others note that prophetic poetry speaks in the strongest terms to break through complacency. Critical scholars often add that the book gathers words from different moments, some spoken before the fall and some shaped after it.

On any reading the tension is deliberate: the judgment is total enough to end the old order, and God's mercy is deep enough that the end is not final.
passages.asks: Jeremiah wanted to weep for his people and also to run away from them. Ask whether you know that tension with your own family, church or town. And ask how you speak: whether your words of peace match what is in your heart.

passages.t: Wailing women, and boast only in knowing the LORD
passages.happening:
God tells the people to summon the wailing women, the most skillful, to come quickly and raise a lament (verse 17), so that their eyes overflow with tears (verse 18). The cry of ruin is heard from Zion (verse 19). The women are to teach their daughters to wail, and one another to lament (verse 20). ‘For death has climbed in through our windows’ (verse 21). It has cut off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares (verse 21). Bodies will fall like cut grain behind the reaper, with no one to gather them (verse 22).

Then a different word. ‘Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches’ (verse 23). ‘But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth’ (verse 24).

The days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised in the body but not in the heart: Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert peoples, and the whole house of Israel, uncircumcised in heart (verses 25 and 26).
passages.hearers:
Professional mourning women were a fixture of funerals across the ancient Near East. They were skilled in chanting laments with set forms and refrains, and a grieving family would hire them to lead the wailing. God tells the women to teach their daughters, which meant that death would be so common the skill would be needed in every home.

Death climbing through the windows is a picture of something that cannot be locked out. No fortress keeps it away.

Verses 23 and 24 name the three things people boast in: wisdom, strength and wealth. Against them stand the three things God delights in: loving devotion, justice and righteousness. To know God is to know a God like that.

Verses 25 and 26 name Judah's neighbors. Several of them practiced circumcision in some form. The mark in the body meant nothing without the heart it was meant to show, for Judah as for them.
passages.later: Paul quotes verses 23 and 24 twice: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), as also in 2 Corinthians 10:17. Moses had called for the same inward circumcision (Deuteronomy 10:16).
passages.hard:
Death climbs in through the windows and cuts off the children from the streets. How should a reader carry that?

The chapter names the deaths of the siege as a horror and grieves them. It summons mourners, not explanations. It does not say the children deserved it, and nothing here gives anyone a warrant to read a child's death, or any people's suffering, as a punishment deserved.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God says to boast only in knowing him. Ask what you are most tempted to boast in: wisdom, strength or money. And ask what it would mean for you to know a God who delights in loving devotion, justice and righteousness.
